title: Schafkopf – rules
sub: Bavaria's national card game: four players, 32 cards and a set of trumps unlike any other – the Ober and Unter always win. Two against two, or one against all.
goal: The goal: together with your partner – or alone in a Solo – take tricks worth at least 61 of the 120 card points.

seo.rulesT: Schafkopf rules – the Bavarian card game explained
seo.rulesD: How to play Schafkopf: dealing, the 14 trumps, card points, Sauspiel, Wenz and Solo, announcing, tricks, scoring with Schneider and Laufende, variants and FAQ.

info.intro: In Bavarian pubs Schafkopf is as much part of the table as the beer. It takes an evening to learn and a lifetime to master. This page explains the standard rules – and you can play with an ordinary French-suited Skat pack if you don't have Bavarian cards.

rules.setupLead: Schafkopf is played by exactly four players with 32 cards: 7, 8, 9, 10, Unter, Ober, King and Ace (called the Sau) in four suits. The Bavarian pack has its own suits – with a French pack you simply translate:
rules.setupP: With a French pack the queen is the Ober and the jack is the Unter. That's how the cards on this page are drawn: Q = Ober, J = Unter, A = Sau.
rules.dealP: The dealer shuffles, lets the player on their right cut and deals clockwise, twice four cards to everyone, so each player holds 8 cards. The player to the dealer's left is called Vorhand: they announce first and lead the first trick. After every game the deal moves one seat to the left.
rules.trLead: In the standard game, the Sauspiel, there are 14 trumps. Every trump beats every card of the other suits.
rules.trAlt: The 14 trumps from highest to lowest: Ober of acorns, leaves, hearts and bells, Unter of acorns, leaves, hearts and bells, then ace, 10, king, 9, 8 and 7 of hearts.
rules.trP: Among the Ober and among the Unter the suit order decides: Eichel beats Gras beats Herz beats Schellen. Important: Ober and Unter are always trumps – they don't belong to their suit any more.
rules.suitP: Eichel, Gras and Schellen each have only six cards left. Within a suit the order is ace (Sau), 10, king, 9, 8, 7 – the 10 is higher than the king.
rules.suitAlt: Order within a suit from high to low: ace, 10, king, 9, 8, 7 of leaves.
rules.ptLead: At the end it's not the number of tricks that counts but the card points (in Bavaria: Augen, eyes) in them:
rules.ptP: Together that makes 120 points. The playing side needs at least 61 to win – with 60 they lose. Ober and Unter are the strongest cards but are worth little; the aces and 10s are what you are after.
rules.gmLead: Before the first card, the players decide what is played. The three basic games, from lowest to highest:
rules.gm_sauP: The player calls an ace (“I play with the Gras-Sau”). Whoever holds it is their partner – but stays secret until the ace appears. You must hold at least one card of the called suit yourself, but not the ace. Hearts can't be called, they are trumps.
rules.gm_wenzP: Only the four Unter are trumps. The Ober go back into their suits between king and 9, and hearts is a normal suit.
rules.gm_soloP: The player chooses a suit, which takes the place of hearts: Ober, Unter and that suit are trumps. Whoever plays a Solo usually holds lots of Ober and Unter.
rules.b1p: Starting with Vorhand, everyone says in turn whether they want to play (“I'd play”) or pass (“weiter”). Each player speaks once.
rules.b2p: If several want to play, the higher game wins: a Solo beats a Wenz, a Wenz beats a Sauspiel. With equal games the player who spoke first wins.
rules.b3p: If everyone passes, the cards are thrown in and the next dealer deals again – or you play a Ramsch.
rules.playLead: Vorhand leads the first trick. Then everyone plays one card in turn, clockwise.
rules.t1p: You have to follow: if a trump is led, play a trump; if a suit is led, play that suit. Ober and Unter don't count as their suit – they are trumps.
rules.t2p: Then you may play any card: trump in or throw away a card of another suit. There is no obligation to trump.
rules.t3p: The highest trump wins the trick. Without a trump, the highest card of the suit that was led wins. The winner takes the four cards and leads the next trick.
rules.trickAlt: Example trick in a Sauspiel with four players
rules.trick3: has no leaves, trumps with the 7 of hearts
rules.trick4: has no leaves either, overtrumps with the Unter of bells
rules.trickNote: Dana's Unter of bells is the lowest Unter, but every Unter beats every heart. She takes the trick – 4 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 6 points – and leads next.
rules.calledP: In a Sauspiel the called ace has to be played the first time its suit is led – it may not be held back or thrown away on another trick (except in the last trick). The partner may only lead that suit without the ace if they hold at least four cards of it (including the ace): that's called running away, and after that the ace is free.
rules.scLead: Schafkopf is traditionally played for small money, but points on paper work just as well. A common tariff, counted per player:
rules.sc3: Schneider: the losers stay below 31 (playing side: 30 or fewer; defenders: 29 or fewer)
rules.sc4: Schwarz: the losers have no trick at all (includes Schneider)
rules.sc5: Laufende: every top trump in an unbroken row from the very top (Eichel-Ober, in a Wenz Eichel-Unter), from 3 (in a Wenz from 2)
rules.scP: Laufende always add to the game value, no matter which side held them – even if the losers had them, they just make the game more expensive. Example: a Sauspiel won with Schneider and three Laufende is worth 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 points.
rules.payP: In a Sauspiel each winner gets the value from one of the losers: two players +5, two players −5. In a Wenz or Solo the single player gets the value from each of the three others – or pays each of them if they lose. In a pub this is often 10 cents for a Sauspiel and 50 cents for a Solo.
rules.varLead: Schafkopf has official tournament rules, but almost every pub has its own extras. Agree on them before the first deal. The most common:
rules.var1: Ramsch: if nobody plays, everyone plays for themselves with the Sauspiel trumps. Whoever takes the most card points loses. Whoever takes every trick (Durchmarsch) wins.
rules.var2: Kontra and Re: before the first card, an opponent may say “Kontra” and double the game. The player can answer with “Re” and double it again.
rules.var3: Tout: in a Solo or Wenz, the player announces they will take every trick. The game counts double (no extra Schneider or Schwarz) – a single lost trick loses it.
rules.var4: Farbwenz: the four Unter plus a chosen suit are trumps; the Ober stay in their suits. Ranks between Sauspiel and Wenz.
rules.var5: Geier: like the Wenz, but only the four Ober are trumps.
rules.var6: Klopfen: after the first four cards, any player may knock on the table – the coming game counts double.
rules.var7: Bettel: the player wants to take no trick at all. There are no trumps, and each suit runs ace, king, Ober, Unter, 10, 9, 8, 7 (the 10 drops below the Unter).
rules.var8: Short pack: without the 7s and 8s, 24 cards, six per player. Faster and full of trumps.
rules.var9: Five at the table: the dealer sits out each game and the seat moves on – so five can play one evening together.
rules.faq1a: The ace. The name comes from old Bavarian cards that showed a sow on the ace. The Gras-Sau is the ace of leaves (spades).
rules.faq2a: No. All Ober and Unter are trumps, whatever suit they show. If Eichel is led in a Sauspiel, you may not follow with the Eichel-Ober – it counts as a trump, see Trumps.
rules.faq3q: Do I have to trump if I can't follow?
rules.faq3a: No. In Schafkopf you only have to follow suit. If you can't, you are free to trump or to throw away any card.
rules.faq4a: The playing side needs 61. With exactly 60 points it has lost.
rules.faq5q: Can I call an ace if I have no card of its suit?
rules.faq5a: No. You need at least one card of the called suit (not counting Ober and Unter), and you may not hold the called ace yourself. With all three aces in your hand you can't play a Sauspiel – think about a Solo instead.
rules.faq6q: What if nobody wants to play?
rules.faq6a: The cards are thrown in and dealt again. Many groups play a Ramsch instead.
rules.faq7q: Can I play Schafkopf with a normal pack of cards?
rules.faq7a: Yes. Use a 32-card Skat pack: clubs for Eichel, spades for Gras, hearts for Herz and diamonds for Schellen, the queens as Ober and the jacks as Unter – see Setup.
rules.faq8a: Real Schafkopf needs four. With three, try Skat, a close cousin with the same 32 cards. With five, the dealer sits out.
